title: Verbs: Kinds, Transitivity and Principal Parts

blocks.text: "The dog smells the meat." "The meat smells bad." Same verb, but in the first sentence the dog is doing something, and in the second nothing is being done at all. The verb is the engine of every sentence, and knowing which kind of engine you are looking at decides what else the sentence is allowed to contain.

blocks.markdown:
A **verb** tells what the subject does, or what the subject is. Every complete sentence needs at least one **finite verb** — a verb that shows tense and agrees with a subject.

Examined at senior secondary level, verbs are tested in three ways:

1. **Kind** — action, linking or auxiliary
2. **Transitivity** — does the verb take an object or not?
3. **Principal parts** — the base form, simple past and past participle, especially of irregular verbs

blocks.title: Linking verb
blocks.text: A verb that expresses no action but joins the subject to a word describing or renaming it: be, become, seem, appear, remain, look, sound, feel, taste, smell, grow, turn. Test it by substituting a form of *be* — if the sentence still makes sense, the verb is linking.

blocks.caption: What each kind of verb allows after it

blocks.markdown:
### Transitivity: ask "what?"

Say the verb and ask **"what?"** or **"whom?"** immediately after it.

- *The driver repaired* — repaired **what**? *the tyre*. There is an object, so the verb is **transitive**.
- *The baby slept* — slept **what**? The question is nonsense. No object, so the verb is **intransitive**.

Be careful: an adverb after the verb is not an object. In *The choir sang beautifully*, *beautifully* answers "how", not "what", so the verb is intransitive. In *The choir sang the anthem*, there is a real object, so the same verb is transitive.

blocks.title: Untangling the verbs students confuse most
blocks.prompt: Decide the correct verb: "The government has once again (risen / raised) the pump price of petrol."

steps.text: Identify the two candidate verbs and their principal parts. *Rise* gives rise, rose, risen. *Raise* gives raise, raised, raised.
Check transitivity. *Rise* is intransitive — something goes up on its own. *Raise* is transitive — somebody lifts something.
Look for an object in the sentence. *The pump price of petrol* is clearly acted upon, so an object is present.
Since an object is present, the transitive verb *raise* is required.
*Has* demands a past participle, and the participle of *raise* is *raised*.
Apply the same reasoning to the twin pairs: lie/lay, sit/set, fall/fell. The first of each pair is intransitive; the second is transitive.

blocks.answer: raised — the transitive verb is needed because the sentence has an object, and *has* requires the participle form

blocks.caption: Principal parts examiners return to year after year

blocks.title: The participle needs an auxiliary
blocks.text: Never use a past participle on its own as the main verb of a sentence. "He begun the work" and "They gone home" are wrong. Write "He **has** begun the work" and "They **have** gone home", or use the simple past: "He began the work."

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: When a question offers you two similar verbs, look for an object first. If the sentence has something being acted upon, choose the transitive verb of the pair — laid, raised, set, felled. If nothing is acted upon, choose the intransitive one — lain, risen, sat, fallen.

points: Verbs are action, linking or auxiliary, and each kind controls what may follow it.
Ask "what?" after the verb to test transitivity; an adverb is not an object.
The same verb can be transitive in one sentence and intransitive in another.
Learn the three principal parts of irregular verbs, especially lie/lay and rise/raise.
A past participle must have an auxiliary such as *has*, *have* or *had* in front of it.
